steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper presenting a new multilingual dataset of webcam eye-tracking recorded while people read texts and answer questions. Motivate why eye-tracking data helps NLP, explain the limits of existing eye-tracking datasets, and describe how our dataset was collected and the reading tasks used.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- Why eye movement data is useful for NLP
- How gaze data has been used in NLP models
- Limits of existing eye-tracking datasets
- Our dataset: WebQAmGaze and how it was collected
- The two reading tasks and our hypothesis

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
## Introduction

- Why eye movement data is useful for NLP
  - direct access to human language processing signals (cite)
  - augment models with human inductive bias (cite); evaluate/analyze inner workings, explainability (cite)
  - ML models in many fields -> need to explain predictions (cite)
  - where readers look when searching for an answer -> transparency/explainability for QA models
- Gaze in NLP models
  - natural reading data improved: document summarizing (cite), POS tagging (cite), NER (cite), others
  - engineered reading time features: number, location, duration of fixations; stages of linguistic processing (cite)
  - added as extra input to ML models
  - correlate with attention in computational models (cite) -> attention models like BERT, weigh attention layer with gaze (cite), better task performance
- Limits of existing datasets
  - need large text datasets; eye-tracking datasets small, expensive equipment, lab participants
  - sparse; most stimuli in English
  - task-specific: different gaze patterns depending on priming, e.g. linguistic annotation vs information-seeking (cite)
  - hard to transfer to other domains/tasks; open question normal vs task-specific reading for NLP
- WebQAmGaze
  - multilingual webcam eye-tracking-while-reading dataset; reading research, low- vs high-quality gaze comparison, ML-based NLP
  - crowd-sourcing: Amazon Mechanical Turk and Cognition; jsPsych (cite), WebGazer (cite)
  - texts in English, Spanish, German, Turkish from open-source QA dataset
  - data + experiment/analysis code online
- Two paradigms
  - normal reading (NR): read text, answer comprehension question on next screen
  - information-seeking (IS): question first, then text, then question again
  - IS: faster reading, higher omission rates, fewer words fixated (cite); lower alignment with NLP models (cite)
  - both tasks -> analyze this in webcam recordings
  - hypothesis: more fixations on relevant target spans -> correct answers

steps.text:
## Introduction

Eye movement data is useful for natural language processing (NLP) models, because it gives direct access to signals of human language processing. Eye-tracking recordings can be used to augment NLP models by giving them a human inductive bias, or to evaluate and analyze how the models work inside and make them more explainable. As machine learning models appear in many fields of application, there is a need to explain the predictions of these models. More concretely, where readers look when they search for the answer to a question in a text can give information that helps to ensure transparency and explainability in computational models of question-answering.

Eye movement data recorded during natural reading has been used to improve models for various NLP tasks, such as document summarizing, part of speech tagging, and named entity recognition, and others. The eye movements are turned into engineered reading time features, like the number, location, and duration of fixations, which reflect the different stages of linguistic processing during language comprehension. These features are then added as extra input to the machine learning models for the NLP tasks. Reading time features have been shown to correlate with the attention mechanism in computational language processing models. Because of this, it is natural to move to attention models like BERT, where the eye-tracking features can directly be used to weigh the attention layer and improve the task performance of the model.

- Limits of existing datasets
  - need large text data; eye-tracking datasets small, expensive equipment, lab participants
  - sparse, mostly English stimuli
  - task-specific reading (annotation vs information-seeking) -> hard to transfer; normal vs task-specific for NLP?
- WebQAmGaze
  - multilingual webcam eye-tracking-while-reading dataset: reading research, low- vs high-quality gaze, NLP applications
  - Amazon Mechanical Turk and Cognition, jsPsych, WebGazer
  - English, Spanish, German, Turkish texts from open-source QA dataset; data and code online
- Two paradigms
  - NR: text then comprehension question; IS: question, text, question again
  - IS: faster reading, more omissions; lower alignment with NLP models
  - hypothesis: more fixations on target spans -> correct answers

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Eye movement data is useful for natural language processing (NLP) models, because it gives direct access to signals of human language processing. Eye-tracking recordings can be used to augment NLP models by giving them a human inductive bias, or to evaluate and analyze how the models work inside and make them more explainable. As machine learning models appear in many fields of application, there is a need to explain the predictions of these models. More concretely, where readers look when they search for the answer to a question in a text can give information that helps to ensure transparency and explainability in computational models of question-answering.

Eye movement data recorded during natural reading has been used to improve models for various NLP tasks, such as document summarizing, part of speech tagging, and named entity recognition, and others. The eye movements are turned into engineered reading time features, like the number, location, and duration of fixations, which reflect the different stages of linguistic processing during language comprehension. These features are then added as extra input to the machine learning models for the NLP tasks. Reading time features have been shown to correlate with the attention mechanism in computational language processing models. Because of this, it is natural to move to attention models like BERT, where the eye-tracking features can directly be used to weigh the attention layer and improve the task performance of the model.

However, these machine learning approaches need large text datasets, so they are often limited by the size and availability of the existing eye-tracking datasets. Collecting these datasets needs expensive equipment and participants who are present in a lab. Datasets are also sparse, and most reading stimuli are still collected in English. It is also common that datasets provide a specific reading task, because different gaze patterns come up depending on what task participants are primed on, e.g., reading during linguistic annotation or information-seeking reading. So it is hard to transfer eye movement measures from specific datasets to other domains or tasks. It also raises the question of whether eye movement data from normal reading or from task-specific reading is more useful for NLP models.

Because of these challenges, in this work we present WebQAmGaze, a multilingual webcam eye-tracking-while-reading dataset. It is made to be used for reading research and for comparing low-quality and high-quality gaze recordings, but also in machine learning-based NLP applications. To make a large-scale experiment setup possible, we collect the data through the crowd-sourcing platforms Amazon Mechanical Turk and Cognition, together with the open-source libraries jsPsych and WebGazer. To make sure the text stimuli are suitable for downstream NLP applications, we select texts in multiple languages (English, Spanish, German, and Turkish) from an open-source question-answering dataset. The WebQAmGaze data and the related experiment and analysis code are available online.

We use two experiment paradigms for collecting the data. In the normal reading (NR) task, participants read a continuous text and answer a comprehension question on the next screen. In the information-seeking (IS) task, participants first see the question they have to answer, then the text itself, and then the question again. Previous work has shown that information-seeking reading leads to faster reading speed and higher omission rates, i.e., fewer words are fixated during this kind of search task compared to normal reading. This type of reading also aligns less with NLP models. Since we collect eye-tracking data from both tasks, it is possible to analyze this behavior in webcam recordings. Our hypothesis is that more fixations on the relevant target spans in the text will result in participants answering the questions correctly.

The eye movements are turned into engineered reading time features, like the number, location, and duration of fixations, which reflect the different stages of linguistic processing during language comprehension [2]. These features are then added as extra input to the machine learning models for the NLP tasks. Reading time features have been shown to correlate with the attention mechanism in computational language processing models [11]. Because of this, it is natural to move to attention models like BERT, where the eye-tracking features can directly be used to weigh the attention layer [12,13,14] and improve the task performance of the model.

So it is hard to transfer eye movement measures from specific datasets to other domains or tasks. Because of these challenges, in this work we present WebQAmGaze, a multilingual webcam eye-tracking-while-reading dataset. steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
## Introduction

Eye movement data is beneficial for natural language processing (NLP) models because it provides direct access to human language processing signals [1]. Eye-tracking recordings can be leveraged to augment NLP models with a human inductive bias [2,3] or to evaluate and analyze the inner workings of the models and increase their explainability [4,5,6]. With the emergence of machine learning models in many fields of application, the need to explain their predictions arises [7]. More concretely, where readers look when searching for the answer to a question in a text can provide information that ensures transparency and explainability in computational models of question-answering.

Eye movement data recorded from natural reading has been used to improve models for various NLP tasks such as document summarizing [8], part of speech tagging [9], and named entity recognition [10], among others. The eye movements are translated into engineered reading time features, such as the number, location, and duration of fixations, which reflect the various stages of linguistic processing during language comprehension [2]. These features are then included as additional input to the machine learning models. Reading time features have been shown to correlate with the attention mechanism in computational language processing models [11]. Hence, there is a natural jump to attention models such as BERT, where the eye-tracking features can be used directly to weigh the attention layer [12,13,14] and improve the model's task performance.

However, these machine learning approaches rely on large text datasets and are thus often limited by the size and availability of existing eye-tracking datasets, which require expensive equipment and participants present in a lab. Dataset availability is also sparse, with most reading stimuli still collected in English. It is also common for datasets to provide a specific reading task, since different gaze patterns are elicited depending on the task participants are primed on, e.g., reading during linguistic annotation or information-seeking reading [15,16]. Therefore, it is difficult to transfer eye movement measures from specific datasets to other domains or tasks, which also opens the question of whether eye movement data from normal reading or task-specific reading is more beneficial for NLP models.

In light of these challenges, we present WebQAmGaze, a multilingual webcam eye-tracking-while-reading dataset tailored not only for reading research and comparisons between low-quality and high-quality gaze recordings but also for machine learning-based NLP applications. To enable a large-scale experiment setup, the data is collected through the crowd-sourcing platforms Amazon Mechanical Turk and Cognition, paired with the open-source libraries jsPsych [17] and WebGazer [18]. To ensure the adequacy of the text stimuli for downstream NLP applications, we select texts in multiple languages (English, Spanish, German, and Turkish) from an open-source question-answering dataset. The WebQAmGaze data and the related experiment and analysis code are available online.

For the data collection, we employ two experiment paradigms: a normal reading (NR) task, where participants read a continuous text and answer a comprehension question on the next screen, and an information-seeking (IS) task, where participants are shown the question before reading the text, followed by the text itself and the question again. Previous work has shown that information-seeking reading results in faster reading speed and higher omission rates, i.e., fewer words are fixated during such a search task than in normal reading [15]. This type of reading also leads to lower alignment with NLP models [14]. By collecting eye-tracking data from both tasks, we make it possible to analyze this behavior in webcam recordings. We hypothesize that a higher number of fixations on the relevant target spans in the text will result in participants answering the questions correctly.
